title: Day-1 integration catalog
purpose: The connectors and data feeds Maplepot needs so the loop we built in this repo can run against a real estate. The loop has to detect an attacker, divert it, remove its capability, and prove the fix held. Each entry says what data we get, what blue action it unlocks, how we demo it against one of our estates, and why it sits where it does in the order.

prioritization.principle: We rank a connection by how much of the attack chain it lets us cover, and by whether it can both detect and act. A feed that only alerts is worth less than one that also has a kill switch we can pull, and a feed that names the specific route or credential an attacker used is worth more than one that gives us a generic anomaly.

criteria.name: chain coverage
criteria.question: Which link does it cover: initial access, identity, code and CI, artifact, runtime, or the deception route?
criteria.why: A chain is only as useful as the links we can see and break. We already demonstrate a full chain in the parser estate, so the gaps are the integrations.

criteria.name: precision
criteria.question: Can it produce a signal that only an attacker generates?
criteria.why: Our detection thesis is that an attacker-only route or credential beats a behavioral score. We want feeds that can carry that kind of signal.

criteria.name: enforcement power
criteria.question: Can it remove the capability, or only report it?
criteria.why: The rerun showed capability removal is what makes a fix hold on re-attack. Alert-only integrations are supporting acts.

criteria.name: ground truth
criteria.question: Can we read the outcome to score a run?
criteria.why: A held verdict has to come from the estate's recorded state. The integration is often where that state lives.

criteria.name: access cost
criteria.question: Is there a read API and a webhook without an agent install?
criteria.why: Read-first gets us a demo in days, and keeps the change small.

criteria.name: blast radius
criteria.question: What breaks if our action is wrong?
criteria.why: Write actions on identity and CI can take down production. Those start in dry-run with a TTL and an audit trail.

tiers.P0: Day one. These six cover the whole loop end to end: the route, the identity, the code and CI, the artifact, the runtime, and the secret.
tiers.P1: First ninety days. These extend coverage to cloud control planes, endpoints, agents, the alert pipeline, and collaboration surfaces.
tiers.P2: Later. Useful for breadth, deception placement, and prioritization, but not needed to show the loop working.

prioritization.day1_demo: The smallest credible demo uses one attacker route through a proxy, one stolen identity at the IdP, one poisoned artifact at a registry, one canary secret in a vault, and one kernel denial at runtime. That combination lets us show the whole loop, detection to diversion to capability removal to a held re-attack, against the OpenAI and ChainDrop shapes we already run.

correlation.note: Detection, containment, and verification only line up if the integrations agree on a set of identifiers. We ask every connector for these keys up front, even when it means mapping them ourselves, because a canary hit that cannot be tied to a session cannot trigger the right containment or prove the fix held.

join_keys.used_for: Bind a detection to the exact route that must be diverted or denied.
Tie a browser session to a canary touch and to a later containment action.
Resolve a user across the IdP, code host, vault, and cloud.
Revoke the exact credential an attacker replayed.
Gate a connected AI agent and revoke its connector separately from the user.
Contain the process that read the canary or made the connection.
Quarantine a release and prove the real registry stayed clean.
Revoke or rotate the credential that was read.
Mark our planted credential, document, or hostname so any use is unambiguous.
Attach every signal and action to one replay so the report is reproducible.

guardrails: Read-only first. Every connector starts with the smallest read scope, and write access is a separate grant we add only for a specific demo.
Dry-run enforcement. Show what a control would do, on a copy, before it touches live traffic.
Blast-radius query before action. Report how many workloads, users, or routes a selector would hit, and refuse above a threshold without a human.
Reversible with a TTL. Every applied control carries an expiry and a one-call rollback.
Full audit trail. The signal, the decision, the action, and the outcome are logged together and replayable.
No credential retention. We read token metadata where the API allows it, and we never store the token itself.

integrations.name: Reverse proxy, API gateway, service mesh, and DNS
integrations.why_priority: This is the control point where route-bound deception is wired. A route that no legitimate principal uses gives us an attacker signal with no false positives, and the same box can send that route to the decoy. Without it, our best idea stays a lab fixture.

apis: Envoy access log service and tap

enforcement: route the attacker route to a decoy
taint the session so its later requests stay on the decoy
deny egress from a tainted route

demo.incident: openai-hacktron, and the parser estate we already run
demo.run: Wire a route that legitimate clients never take to the maplepot. Send a legitimate client down the sanctioned route and an attacker down the canary route.
demo.proves: The real target stays untouched and the decoy records the hit. The legitimate client is unaffected. We show the route decision, the decoy hit, and the empty real state in one report.

risks: Inline blocking can break real traffic if the route map is wrong
TLS fingerprinting needs a termination point we control
integrations.fallback: Start in monitor mode and emit the would-be divert decision as an alert.

integrations.name: Identity provider and OAuth or OIDC plane
integrations.why_priority: Identity is the pivot in four of our catalog incidents, and it is where the kill switch lives. It gives us the cross-tier redemption signal, the token replay signal, and the ability to revoke the exact grant an attacker is using. Nothing else does both halves.

apis: Okta System Log API and OAuth grants API
Entra sign-in and audit logs plus Microsoft Graph

enforcement: revoke a refresh token or the whole grant
sign out the sessions for a user
require step-up before a cross-tier redemption
block cross-tier redemption at the policy layer

demo.run: Replay a stolen refresh token from a new device. Serve the decoy integration so the token reaches canary records, then revoke the grant and turn on segmentation, and re-attack.
demo.proves: The cross-tier redemption fires as a high-precision detection, the decoy returns canary data, the revoke and segmentation void the replay, and the re-attack fails while a benign sign-in control still works.

risks: Revoking the wrong grant logs out real users
Log schemas differ enough that the join keys need mapping
integrations.fallback: Read logs only and drive enforcement through the app's own IdP.

integrations.name: Source control and CI/CD
integrations.why_priority: The supply-chain step and the connected-agent pivot both live here. It is the ground truth for whether a merge or a publish landed, and it is where an agent's action can be gated before it ships.

events: pull request opened, reviewed, and merged
fields: issue or PR title and body
apis: GitHub webhooks, audit log, Actions API, OIDC

enforcement: require a second reviewer for a protected path
block a publish from a non-CI identity
gate an agent action that came from a non-interactive session
revoke an app or personal token

demo.run: Replay an attacker-controlled issue title into a workflow, then drive a connected agent to publish. Show the injection alert, the gated publish, and a re-attack that fails.
demo.proves: The attacker action is detected by actor type and trigger, the publish is refused without a CI identity, the agent pivot is gated, and the benign maintainer PR still merges.

risks: Write access to repos or workflows is sensitive
Many events, so we need to filter to the ones that matter
integrations.fallback: Read-only audit log and webhooks, with enforcement left to existing branch protection.

integrations.name: Package and artifact registry
integrations.why_priority: This is the worm's goal and the easiest place to put a decoy that absorbs it. It gives us the publish event, the identity behind it, and the provenance, and it is where we can serve a canary registry that a harvest touches and the real one stays clean.
enforcement: serve a decoy registry for a canary token

demo.run: The install hook harvests a canary token. The publish goes to the decoy registry, and rak denies the credential read and the egress.
demo.proves: The real registry records no poisoned release, the decoy records the attempt, the canary use is a tripwire, and a benign CI publish still succeeds.

risks: A decoy registry has to be trusted by the client, usually through DNS or a token scoped to the decoy
Yanking a package can break downstream builds

integrations.name: Runtime telemetry and kernel enforcement
integrations.why_priority: This is the last mile. Our rerun showed that capability removal is what makes a fix hold, and a policy on the process is the control that does it without patching the bug. It is also the feed that confirms a canary file was actually read.
enforcement: deny a file read by inode
deny an exec outside the allowlist

demo.incident: openai-hacktron and nextjs-libheif-avif, via the parser estate
demo.run: The decoder is hijacked and we want it contained. Apply the rak policy and re-run the exploit.
demo.proves: The hijack still lands, the secret read and the egress are denied in the kernel, the account takeover never happens, and the benign decode shows no denials.

risks: Broad host access and a privileged sensor
A wrong policy can break a workload, so it needs a dry-run mode
integrations.fallback: Auditd or an unprivileged eBPF collector, with enforcement through rak's Landlock path.

integrations.name: Secrets manager and credential vault
integrations.why_priority: Canary credentials are the cheapest high-precision tripwire we have, and the vault is where we revoke the one an attacker stole. It closes the credential access link in the chain and gives us a clean detection with no false positives.
enforcement: plant a canary secret on the attacker route
deny a read by inode at runtime

demo.run: Plant a canary secret where only an attacker would reach it. The worm or the RCE reads it, we revoke and rotate, and then re-attack.
demo.proves: The canary read is a detection, the decoy value is worthless, the revoke takes effect, and the re-attack cannot read the secret.

risks: Rotation can break a running app
A canary secret has to look real enough to be worth reading
integrations.fallback: Static canary files watched by the runtime feed.

integrations.name: Cloud control plane and cloud identity
examples: Microsoft Azure Activity and Defender for Cloud
Google Cloud Audit Logs and SCC
integrations.why_priority: It is the second half of the identity chain. Once an attacker owns an identity, the cloud control plane is how it reaches Key Vaults, storage, and VMs. We need it to see that move and to revoke the workload identity.
enforcement: attach a deny policy to a session
apply an SCP or permission boundary

demo.run: Replay a compromised identity making control-plane calls toward a decoy key vault and storage account.
demo.proves: The control-plane anomaly is detected, the decoy resources absorb the access, the deny policy stops the session, and a benign admin action is unaffected.

risks: High-privilege read scope
Control-plane log volume is large
integrations.fallback: Read-only logs with enforcement through the identity provider.

integrations.name: Endpoint detection and response
integrations.why_priority: The npm and developer-tool incidents land on workstations, not servers. Endpoint telemetry is how we see a lifecycle script spawn a shell on a developer's machine, and it is where we can isolate the host.

demo.run: Run the stand-in worm on a developer workstation image and watch the endpoint feed.
demo.proves: The lifecycle script and the credential file reads show up as a process lineage, the host isolates cleanly, and the clean install produces no alert.

risks: Agent deployment and host access
Endpoint actions are disruptive
integrations.fallback: eBPF on the build runner, which covers most of the CI half.

integrations.name: AI agent gateway, MCP registry, and coding assistants
integrations.why_priority: A connected agent is a new privileged principal, and several catalog incidents treat it as the pivot. We need the agent's identity and its tool calls, separate from the user's, to gate an action that came from a hijacked session.

apis: MCP server registry and tool listing

enforcement: gate an agent action that came from a non-interactive session
put the agent process on an egress allowlist

demo.run: Feed a poisoned tool description to an agent, then gate its privileged action and contain its process.
demo.proves: The poisoned tool call is detected, the gated action is refused, the agent cannot read the credential files or reach the exfiltration endpoint, and a normal tool call still works.

risks: The space moves fast and APIs are unstable
Prompt payloads are large and sensitive
integrations.fallback: Contain the agent as a process with the runtime feed and leave tool-level detection for later.

integrations.name: SIEM and SOAR
integrations.why_priority: Our alerts are only useful when they reach the tools a security team already watches, and the response playbooks are the natural place to trigger containment. It is the integration that makes the product fit an existing workflow.
enforcement: enrich an alert with asset and identity context

demo.run: Push the D2, D4, D5, and D6 alerts from a parser-estate run into the SIEM and run a playbook.
demo.proves: The alerts arrive with the join keys intact, the playbook fires the containment action, and the re-attack result lands back on the same case.

risks: Alert schema mapping per platform
Ingestion cost at volume
integrations.fallback: A webhook and a plain JSON schema that any platform can ingest.

integrations.name: Collaboration and email
integrations.why_priority: These surfaces carry the breadcrumbs and the data that attackers go after next. A canary document or a honey credential in a share is easy to plant and gives a clean signal when it is touched, and the same feed shows the exfiltration attempt.

demo.incident: the identity and collab stages of openai-hacktron and klue-oauth-icarus
demo.run: Plant a canary document in a shared drive and a honey credential in a message, then let the attacker identity touch them.
demo.proves: The touch produces a high-precision alert tied to the session, the share and the credential are revoked, and a legitimate user opening the same folder produces nothing.

risks: Privacy and data handling, since content is sensitive
Planted canaries need lifecycle management

integrations.name: SaaS security posture and CASB
integrations.why_priority: It tells us which third-party apps hold which scopes, which is exactly the OAuth supply-chain risk in two catalog incidents. It is valuable context, but the core detection can run without it.

demo.run: Inventory the connected apps, find the over-scoped integration, and revoke it during the replay.
demo.proves: The over-scoped app is found before the replay, the revoke removes the path, and the re-attack fails.

risks: Read scope across all SaaS apps
integrations.fallback: Manual app inventory from the IdP.

integrations.name: Network policy and firewalls
integrations.why_priority: It is how we wall off the real estate once a canary fires and how we enforce an egress allowlist. It supports the diversion story and does not create it, so it sits after the proxy.
enforcement: wall off the real target for a tainted session

demo.run: After the canary fires, deny the tainted workload any route to the real target and re-run the attack.
demo.proves: The attack is contained, the decoy is the only reachable service, and the held verdict comes from the real state.

risks: A bad rule can cause an outage
integrations.fallback: Host-level egress policy through the runtime feed.

integrations.name: Asset inventory, vulnerability, and SBOM
integrations.why_priority: By itself it neither detects nor stops anything. It tells us where to put a decoy and how wide a control would land, which makes the loop safer at scale.

demo.run: Before applying a control, ask which assets it would hit and which asset is worth decoying.
demo.proves: The blast-radius number is attached to the control decision, and the decoy lands on the asset an attacker would want.

risks: Data quality, since stale inventories give wrong answers
integrations.fallback: A hand-maintained asset list for the demo estate.

integrations.name: Privileged access management and bastion
integrations.why_priority: The admin path is a later hop in several chains. Recording privileged sessions and terminating one is useful, but it is not where the first three links live.

demo.run: Replay an attacker using a checked-out credential on a bastion and terminate the session mid-chain.
demo.proves: The privileged session is recorded and cut, and the legitimate operator's session is untouched.

risks: Cutting a session can interrupt remediation work

integrations.name: Threat intelligence and exploited-vulnerability feeds
integrations.why_priority: It decides what we emulate next, not what we block. We already keep a curated incident catalog in this repo, and a feed automates the refresh.

demo.run: Refresh the incident catalog from the feed and pick the next estate to build.
demo.proves: The catalog stays current and every test estate traces to a real incident.

risks: Feed noise
Duplicate incidents
integrations.fallback: The manual catalog in this repo.

day1_stack.summary: Five vendor integrations carry the day-one demo, with two pieces below them doing the enforcement. Together they cover the attacker's entry, its escalation, the artifact it poisons, the credential it steals, and the point where we redirect it.

products.why: The System Log API gives sign-in and OAuth token events with session and token ids, and the Grants API revokes the exact grant an attacker replayed. The free Developer Edition makes the demo reproducible.
products.demo_path: Okta Developer tenant, an OAuth app with read scopes and one revoke scope.

products.why: Webhooks, the Audit Log API, and Actions OIDC claims give actor, actor type, workflow, runner identity, and the trigger event, which is what the injection and agent-pivot detections need. Three of our incidents are GitHub-shaped.
products.demo_path: A free org, webhooks, and a fine-grained token for the audit log.

products.why: Artifactory is enforceable. Publish webhooks, audit, permission targets, and an API to quarantine a version or revoke a token. You already have maple-real-artifactory, so this reuses your own lab.
products.demo_path: Artifactory OSS or trial, with npm public for the ChainDrop surface.

products.why: The cleanest canary primitive. Audit devices log every read with the accessor identity, and leases give us revoke and rotate. It is already in the Artifactory lab.
products.demo_path: Vault dev server with a file audit device.

products.why: The deception control point. ext_authz gives the decision hook, ALS gives the request and route data, and two upstream clusters give the divert. Free, local, and it is the standard mesh data plane.
products.demo_path: Envoy OSS with two clusters and ext_authz to our service.

enforcement_layer.role: File deny by inode, exec allowlist, and egress deny on the untrusted process. This is what makes a fix hold without patching the bug.
Runtime telemetry from eBPF plus in-kernel enforcement, so the signal and the containment come from the same layer. CrowdStrike Falcon is the buyer-facing swap when the customer already runs it.

day1_stack.dependency_note: The route integration assumes the customer's proxy can call us for a decision. If it cannot be changed, the fallback is DNS-based routing, where a canary hostname resolves to the decoy. That is why Cloudflare and Route 53 stay warm.

strongest_demo.name: The release that never shipped
strongest_demo.why_strongest: The outcome is binary, so nobody has to interpret a score. Either a poisoned package ships or it does not, and every product in the path is one the buyer already runs.
steps: A scripted attacker runs on a build runner and reads a Vault credential. The Vault audit fires, and the credential is a canary, so the read is a tripwire with no false positives.
Envoy calls our service through ext_authz when the attacker tries to publish. It sees a canary credential on a route no legitimate CI uses, and routes the publish to the decoy Artifactory cluster.
A reach for the real secret and the real registry gets denied. rak blocks the file read by inode and blocks egress, and Tetragon records the denial.
Okta flags the anomalous grant or the cross-tier redemption that got the attacker this far.
Ground truth settles it. Artifactory's real repo has no new package, the decoy repo has it, Vault's real secret is untouched, and GitHub shows no protected merge.
A re-attack with the same scripted worm fails, and a benign CI publish still succeeds.
strongest_demo.money_shot: Real registry clean, decoy registry poisoned, Vault canary read, kernel denial. Detection, diversion, capability removal, and a held re-attack on one screen, against products the buyer knows.

runner_up_demo.name: The hijacked agent that could not ship
products: an agent surface such as MCP, LiteLLM, or the customer's Copilot
runner_up_demo.why: It is the differentiated story, because a borrowed agent identity is new to most audiences. It is also harder to land in thirty seconds than a poisoned release.
steps: A poisoned issue or tool description points a connected agent at a protected publish.
GitHub identifies the actor as an agent and flags the non-interactive trigger.
We gate the action and revoke the connector, so the publish is refused.
The repo stays clean, and rak contains the agent process.

choice_notes.because: A faster free tenant and a cleaner log-and-grants API. Choose Entra when the buyer is Microsoft-centric.
Raw npm cannot quarantine or revoke the way a private registry can, so the containment half of the demo is weaker. npm stays as the recognizable public surface.
A dev server, exact read events, and leases. Cloud secret managers are a P2 extension.
Local, free, and it has the decision hook. Choose Cloudflare when the customer is SaaS-first and we want DNS-based route-bound deception.
Free and local. Swap in CrowdStrike for the pitch and for real deployments.

deferred.reason: Alert plumbing. It adds nothing to the demo, so we add it after the loop is solid.
Useful for blast radius and decoy placement, not for the first screen.
Add AWS CloudTrail as the first extension once the five are in.
